summary: Defines an XML format for presence authorization rules, which state what presence information may be given to which watchers and when. Clients can manipulate such documents using XCAP. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A list of who may see if you are online and when.

questions: how to control who sees presence info
what is polite blocking in sip presence
what is sub-handling in presence rules
how does xcap manage presence rules
subtitle: An XML format that lets a user say which watchers may see which presence details, and when.

tldr.problem: Presence information is sensitive, and a presence agent needs the presentity's permission before it hands that information to a watcher. Servers and clients need a shared document format for expressing that permission.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5025 builds on the common policy framework. Each rule has conditions (who and when), actions (accept, confirm or block the subscription) and transformations (which parts of the presence document the watcher may see). The document can be managed over XCAP.
tldr.outcome: Every permission is a positive grant, so a missing or misunderstood rule can only reveal less. The cost is that combining rules can give results users do not expect.

today: RFC 5025 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the presence rules format that the XCAP usage pres-rules carries.

sections.title: Why Presence Needs Authorization Rules
sections.content:
In the SIP-based presence system, a user called a watcher subscribes to another user, the presentity, to learn their presence information. A presence agent handles the subscription. Because presence information is sensitive, the agent needs the presentity's authorization before handing it out.

RFC 5025 defines the document format for that authorization, called a presence authorization document. It uses the policy framework of RFC 4745 (common policy), where a policy is a set of rules. Each rule has conditions, actions and transformations. Conditions say when the rule applies, actions tell the server what to do, and transformations say how the presence data is changed (filtered) before the watcher sees it.
sections.eli5: Your friends can ask to see whether you are online. Before the server tells them, it wants to check your rules. This document is how you write those rules down.

sections.title: Structure of a Presence Authorization Document
sections.content:
A presence authorization document is an XML document that follows the schema of RFC 4745. It inherits the MIME type of common policy documents, application/auth-policy+xml. Each rule holds conditions, actions and transformations.

Each action or transformation is called a permission, and every permission is a positive grant of information to the watcher. That gives a well-defined way to combine permissions from several sources. It is also privacy safe, because the lack of any action or transformation can only result in less information being presented to a watcher.

The RFC fills in the usage-specific details that the framework leaves open: how a watcher's identity is worked out, how the sphere condition is computed, one new action, and a set of new transformations.
sections.eli5: Everything on the list is a yes. Nothing on the list means no. So if a rule gets lost, nobody sees more than you meant them to.

sections.title: Conditions: Who the Watcher Is
sections.content:
The identity condition needs a definition of acceptable authentication and a way to turn the watcher into a URI. A SIP request counts as authenticated if the watcher proves its identity cryptographically (for example with a shared secret or a certificate), or if a trusted sender asserts the identity, claims it used cryptographic authentication, and gives the identity as a URI. Examples given are SIP digest authentication, cryptographically verified identity assertions (RFC 4474) and assertions in closed networks (RFC 3325).

Anonymous authentication as described in RFC 3261 does not count, because it yields no identity. Such a request is unauthenticated and matches only an empty identity element. A request that is anonymous only because of a Privacy header still uses its asserted identity.

With digest authentication, a username scoped within a realm is bound by provisioning to an Address of Record (AOR), and that AOR is the watcher URI. Aliases of one user are not related to each other, and URIs of different schemes are never equivalent, so a SIP URI containing a phone number does not match a tel URI with the same number.

The sphere condition is computed from the person data in the presentity's published presence documents. If at least one carries it and all agree, that value is used; otherwise it is undefined. Because sphere changes dynamically, using it to decide subscription handling can suddenly terminate a subscription, so it is mainly useful for transformation rules.
sections.eli5: The server has to be sure who is asking, like a doorman checking ID. Someone with no ID at all only gets in if your list says anyone is welcome.

sections.title: Actions: Subscription Handling
sections.content:
The one action defined here is sub-handling, an enumerated integer that decides what the server does with a subscription and whether to use "polite blocking". The four values are block (0, the default), confirm (10), polite-block (20) and allow (30).

A block value does not guarantee the subscription is denied. If any matching rule has a higher value, the subscription gets the treatment of the maximum of those values, following the combining rules of RFC 4745. A future action must be a new element rather than a change to sub-handling, and when both apply, the least restrictive result wins.

The server's behavior follows the subscription state machine in RFC 3857. A change to block terminates affected subscriptions with a NOTIFY whose reason is rejected, and a new subscription gets a 403 response. With confirm, an active subscription moves back to pending, and a new one gets a 202 response followed by a NOTIFY with state pending and no presence document. A change to polite-block or allow approves a pending subscription, and a new subscription gets a 200 OK followed by a NOTIFY with state active and a presence document.
sections.eli5: For each person you pick one of four answers: no, ask me first, pretend I am offline, or yes. If two of your rules disagree, the friendlier answer wins.

sections.title: Transformations: What the Watcher May See
sections.content:
Transformations drive the privacy filtering of the presence document. The first group is coarse-grained: provide-devices, provide-persons and provide-services choose which device, person and service occurrences are included. Each is a set whose members identify occurrences by class, occurrence ID, and, depending on the element, device ID, service URI or service URI scheme. Sets from different rules are combined by union. The special values all-devices, all-persons and all-services select everything.

The second group controls individual attributes once an element is included. Most are Boolean: provide-activities, provide-class, provide-deviceID, provide-mood, provide-place-is, provide-place-type, provide-privacy, provide-relationship, provide-sphere, provide-status-icon, provide-time-offset and provide-note. If FALSE, the attribute is removed. Some information is always reported, such as the contact, basic status and timestamp of each tuple.

provide-user-input is an enumerated integer: false (0) removes the element, bare (10) keeps it without its idle-threshold and since attributes, thresholds (20) keeps only idle-threshold, and full (30) keeps everything.

provide-unknown-attribute grants access to an attribute, named by name and ns, that the server has no authorization schema for. If the server is later upgraded and learns that schema, the permission is ignored, which stays privacy safe but may surprise. provide-all-attributes is a macro that grants every attribute of the occurrences already included.
sections.eli5: Besides who gets in, you choose what they can see: your phone, your laptop, your mood, your note. Each one is a switch you turn on for that person.

sections.title: Extensibility, XCAP Usage and Requirements
sections.content:
Future permissions must live in a different namespace, and the schema and its namespace MUST NOT be altered, because changes could cause privacy violations through misinterpretation. Since servers ignore unknown permissions, the XCAP capabilities document at the server SHOULD list the namespaces the presence server supports, so a client can check before building a document.

Section 9 defines the XCAP usage. The application unique ID is pres-rules, the default namespace is urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:pres-rules, and documents live under pres-rules/users/ beneath the XCAP root. A single document SHOULD be named index. By default only a user can read or change their own documents.

Servers MUST support all the conditions, actions and transformations defined here, since no mechanism exists to discover a subset. Clients are only RECOMMENDED to support all of them. The RFC also requires that the delivered presence document D satisfy D = F(D), where F is the privacy filter, so filtering again changes nothing. It does not mandate where in processing the filter is applied.
sections.eli5: New kinds of switches can be added later, but only in a separate box, so the old switches never change meaning.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Authorization documents are very sensitive because they show which users someone "likes" or "dislikes". Transport SHOULD be encrypted and SHOULD provide authenticity and message integrity, since an attacker who modifies a document can disrupt the service in subtle ways. When XCAP is used, clients and servers MUST implement HTTP over TLS and HTTP Digest authentication, and sites SHOULD define the root services URI as an https URI.

Because all permissions are positive grants, failure to obtain or understand a document can only reveal less. A consequence is that combining documents can surprise users: if one document allows everyone in example.com and another blocks joe@example.com, joe still receives presence. User interface designers are encouraged to pay attention to combined results. Clients SHOULD also show users rules they do not understand, so users know what is in force.

IANA registers the pres-rules XCAP application usage ID, an XML namespace and an XML schema.
sections.eli5: Your list says who you like and dislike, so it must travel in a locked box. And remember that a yes in one place can beat a no in another.

items.label: confirm
items.desc: Hold the subscription as pending and wait for the presentity.

items.label: polite-block
items.desc: Active, but the document shows the presentity as unavailable.
